title: dedicated-gpu-pool-scheduling-autoscale-warmup-debug-scratchpad-17
content:
Investigating repeated capacity thrash during Dedicated GPU pool warmup (pool: dedicated-a)

Goal: capture commands run, logs/snippets, hypotheses, and next steps for debugging. Personal notes / breadcrumbs so others can pick up.

Summary of symptom:
- During a traffic spike (2026-02-24 02:10-02:35 UTC) dedicated-a pool oscillated between 2 -> 6 -> 1 nodes over ~25m. App-level errors: increased 503s, long queue latency, several model-initialization failures.
- Autoscaler scaling decisions appear to react to queued requests and CPU metrics before model processes are warm. Warmup time for our largest model (m-llama-70b-q4) measured ~7.8s per replica on cold start; expected ~1.5-2s if preloaded.

Commands run (notes + outputs):
1) Check pods & events (k8s):
$ kubectl get pods -n dedicated-pools -l pool=dedicated-a -o wide
NAME                                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
model-serving-m-llama-70b-0                  0/1     Init:0/1   0         3m
model-serving-m-llama-70b-1                  1/1     Running    0         28m
model-warmup-helper-5d9b8                    1/1     Running    0         2h

$ kubectl describe pod model-serving-m-llama-70b-0 -n dedicated-pools
Events:
  Normal  Scheduled  3m   default-scheduler  Successfully assigned dedicated-node-12 to model-serving-m-llama-70b-0
  Normal  Pulling    2m55s  kubelet            Pulling image "registry.redwood/models:m-llama-70b-v2"
  Warning Failed     2m30s kubelet            Failed to allocate device: InsufficientNvidiaGPU
  Warning FailedScheduling 2m30s  default-scheduler  0/10 nodes are available: 6 Insufficient memory, 4 node(s) didn't match node affinity.

Observation: we had intermittent InsufficientNvidiaGPU errors even when autoscaler had recently created nodes. Suspect driver / resource labeling mismatch.

2) Autoscaler logs (k8s deployment redwood-autoscaler, namespace infra):
$ kubectl logs -n infra deploy/redwood-autoscaler --tail=200\[2026-02-24T02:12:10Z] scale up pool dedicated-a: target=6 current=2 reason=queued_requests=123\[2026-02-24T02:14:55Z] started node provisioning node-87 (spot)\[2026-02-24T02:17:02Z] node-87 joined; marking ready\[2026-02-24T02:17:05Z] scale down pool dedicated-a: target=1 current=6 reason=idle_time=5m\[2026-02-24T02:17:06Z] cancelling scale-up for node-89 (provision timed out)

Snippets show scale-up completed then almost immediately scale-down decisions triggered by short idle_time window. Autoscaler policy: scale_down if average_util < 20% for 5m. But warmup time > 5m window across queueing -> leads to thrash.

3) Node logs / kernel driver check (ssh node-87):
$ nvidia-smi -L
GPU 0: NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB (UUID: GPU-aaaa)
$ docker ps --filter name=model-serving -a
CONTAINER ID ... image registry.redwood/models:m-llama-70b-v2  STATUS: Up 4s

No obvious driver errors on node-87. But timing of GPU readiness vs kubelet device plugin might create a race.

4) Warmup helper behavior (we have a warmup job that sends synthetic requests to pre-init models):
$ kubectl logs -n infra job/model-warmup-run-20260224\[INFO] sending 20 warmup requests to model m-llama-70b-v2 replica 0\[INFO] avg model init time: 7800ms (std 1200ms)

5) ML runtime logs (container):
$ kubectl logs model-serving-m-llama-70b-1 -n dedicated-pools\[2026-02-24T02:09:33Z] INFO loading model weights from /mnt/models/m-llama-70b-q4\[2026-02-24T02:09:34Z] INFO initializing attention kernels\[2026-02-24T02:09:36Z] WARN nvrtc compilation fallback: several kernels recompiled at runtime (adds ~300ms)\[2026-02-24T02:10:12Z] INFO model runtime ready (KV cache empty)

6) Scheduler metrics (Prometheus queries saved):
- avg_model_init_time_seconds{pool="dedicated-a",model="m-llama-70b"} = 7.8
- queued_requests_total{pool="dedicated-a"} peaked at 210
- node_provision_time_seconds median = 150 (includes spot startup + kube-provisioner)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Autoscaler scale_down window too aggressive relative to model warmup. Warmup combined with provisioning delays causes replicas to be marked idle -> downscale -> thrash. (High probability)
2) Warmup helper isn't reliably warming every new replica (race: warmup starts before container fully pulled or before GPU plugin ready), so some replicas never reach ready before scale-down. (Medium)
3) Node label/taint mismatch: some new nodes are provisioned with a label gpu.type=rtx-a6000 while deployment requires nvidia.com/gpu=1 and nodeAffinity expects a100 label. This mismatch can cause FailedScheduling -> autoscaler keeps adding nodes -> wasted capacity. (Medium)
4) Model docker image size + pull time + container startup contributes to long start time; using cached images on node (pre-pulled) could reduce latency. (Medium)
5) Spot instance termination / provisioning flakiness (node-89 timed out) led to oscillation. (Low/Medium)

Commands/troubleshooting attempted and results: 
- Increased autoscaler scale_down_grace_period from 300s -> 600s on staging and ran synthetic spike: thrash reduced significantly. (staging test 2026-02-25)
- Instrumented warmup helper to wait for container Ready state before sending requests (added retry + 10s). Observed improved success rate of warmups but still some stalls from image pull times.
- Added labels check in provisioner to ensure node GPU type matches pool model requirements. Found ~3% of nodes created in the time window had wrong label (provisioner bug). Filed JIRA-ENG-4521.
- Tried pre-pulling images via DaemonSet on a subset of nodes -> image pull time reduced from ~40s -> ~5s; however container startup still dominated by model weight load time.
- Tested 'pre-warm' feature: start warmed container on node but keep it idle (no traffic) so kernel caches & nvrtc kernels compiled. Observed init times drop from 7.8s -> 1.9s on subsequent starts. However keeping pre-warm replicas has cost implications.

Error snippets captured: 
- kubelet: "Failed to allocate device: InsufficientNvidiaGPU"
- autoscaler: "cancelling scale-up for node-89 (provision timed out)"
- runtime: "nvrtc compilation fallback: several kernels recompiled at runtime"
- kube-scheduler: "0/10 nodes are available: 6 Insufficient memory, 4 node(s) didn't match node affinity"

Immediate mitigations tried in prod (short-term):
- Bumped scale_down grace window to 10min for dedicated-a (temporary during high-traffic windows).
- Enabled pre-pull DaemonSet for large model images on warm pool nodes.
- Applied a blocker to provisioner to reject mismatched node labels (hotfix).

Open action items / TODOs: 
- [ ] Roll autoscaler config change to all regions (evaluate cost impact) -- owner: Diego
- [ ] Add a 'gpu-ready' probe in warmup orchestration to avoid sending warmup before device plugin ready -- owner: Maya
- [ ] Investigate automated kernel compilation caching (persisted nvrtc cache) in runtime to reduce first-start jitter -- owner: Anya
- [ ] Evaluate cost vs benefit of maintaining a small pool of pre-warmed replicas for top-tier models (A/B test) -- owner: Product/Eng
- [ ] Fix provisioner label bug (JIRA-ENG-4521) and add unit tests -- owner: infra-team

Notes for follow-up:
- Need to capture a full timeline correlated across autoscaler logs + kube events + warmup helper logs. Suggest building a single view (Grafana panel) for dedicated pool incidents: queued requests, scale decisions, node join events, warmup success rate.
- Consider changing scale-down policy to depend on model-warmup-metric (if avg_model_init_time > X, extend grace period automatically).

References / Links: 
- JIRA-ENG-4521 (provisioner labels)
- GH PR infra#1289 (hotfix: reject mismatched node labels)
- Slack thread infra-incident: https://slack.redwood.com/archives/C03INFRA/p1677712345

Scratch notes (ad-hoc):
- Could also try keeping a tiny "standby" replica with weights loaded but process paused (costly but cheap compared to 503s during spikes).
- Check whether old model versions are being pulled (cache miss) due to model-version tag mismatch.
- Add metric: warmup_attempts_success_rate by node to identify nodes where warmup consistently fails.

End of scratchpad.
